params.name: c
params.let: row[1] if row[2] == 1 else row[1] / row[2]

params.name: a
params.choice: [v for v in alist if is_int(v * c) and abs(v * c) <= 10]

params.why: the function must have a constant term

stem: Calculate the $x$-intercept of the graph of $y={=a}\cdot {=b}^{x}{=signed(q)}$. Give the $x$-coordinate of the intercept, rounded to one decimal place.
solution: The $x$-intercept is where the graph cuts the $x$-axis, so we let $y=0$.
Move the constant term to the other side: ${=m}={=a}\cdot {=b}^{x}$.
Divide both sides by ${=a}$ to leave the power on its own: ${=c}={=b}^{x}$.
Now we look for the exponent by trial and error. Try: ${=b}^{{=n0}}={=lo}$ and ${=b}^{{=n0 + 1}}={=hi}$. Since ${=lo}<{=c}<{=hi}$, the exponent $x$ lies between ${=n0}$ and ${=n0 + 1}$.

To round to one decimal place we test the two values halfway to the neighbouring one-decimal values: ${=b}^{{=fixed((2 * t - 1) / 20, 2)}}\approx {=fixed(lo3 / 1000, 3)}$ and ${=b}^{{=fixed((2 * t + 1) / 20, 2)}}\approx {=fixed(hi3 / 1000, 3)}$.

Since ${=fixed(lo3 / 1000, 3)}<{=fixed(c, 3)}<{=fixed(hi3 / 1000, 3)}$, the exponent lies between ${=fixed((2 * t - 1) / 20, 2)}$ and ${=fixed((2 * t + 1) / 20, 2)}$, so $x\approx {=fixed(t / 10, 1)}$ to one decimal place.
notes: Advanced: the book's trial-and-error x-intercept (ex6-8-23b: y = -1/2.4^x + 3, so 6 = 4^x and x is about 1.3) with the harder instances the book's two items do not reach: a fractional or whole-number coefficient of either sign, and a power that is less than 1 (c < 1), so the exponent is negative and the trial values are fractions such as 3^-1 = 1/3. The (b, c) table was computed offline with high-precision logarithms; each row stores b, c as numerator and denominator, the floor of the true exponent, the exponent rounded to tenths as an integer t (so x is about t/10), and b^((t-0.5)/10) and b^((t+0.5)/10) in thousandths. Every row was checked so the true exponent is within 0.031 of t/10, so rounding never sits near a boundary, and so the displayed 3-decimal bounds are strict around c. q is built as -a.c, always a non-zero whole number with |q| at most 10, and a and q always have opposite signs so that c is positive and an x-intercept exists. The solution brackets the exponent between two whole numbers, then confirms the one-decimal answer by testing the two half-way points, which needs no logarithms (not in this book).
